candidates.label: Straight Street, Old City of Damascus
candidates.support: A colonnaded street running east-west through the Old City of Damascus, on the line of the city's main Roman-era street, is traditionally identified with the street called Straight in Acts. Part of it is still known locally as Derb el-Mustakim ("Straight Street"), and today the street is called Souk Medhat Pasha along part of its course, though it is uncertain whether the Derb el-Mustakim name has been used continuously since antiquity.

summary.text: The street called Straight is the Damascus street where, according to Acts, the disciple Ananias found Saul of Tarsus (later the apostle Paul) praying after his encounter on the road to Damascus, and there restored his sight. A colonnaded street on this line still crosses the Old City of Damascus today, part of it still locally called by a name meaning "Straight Street," though it is uncertain whether that name has been used without a break since the first century.

history.text: Acts describes a vision in which the Lord told Ananias to go to "the street which is called Straight" and ask at the house of Judas for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying there after being blinded on the road to Damascus; Ananias obeyed, and Saul's sight was restored.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says that in the Greek period a long, colonnaded street ran through Damascus, "doubtless the 'street which is called Straight,'" running westward from the city's East Gate; part of it is still called Derb el-Mustakim ("Straight Street"), though the encyclopedia does not claim this name has been used without interruption since antiquity.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Syria (ruler: Imperial legates, governed from Antioch)
politicalHistory.note: Administers the Cilician plain throughout, and administered Philip's former tetrarchy directly for a few years after his death (34-37; Antiquities 18.4.6).

Paul writes that "the governor under King Aretas guarded the Damascenes' city" around the time of his escape (2 Corinthians 11:32). How far the Nabataean king Aretas IV actually controlled Damascus is uncertain; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia (1915) cites "a Damascus coin, with the image of King Aretas and the date 101," which, read as the Pompeian era, equals AD 37. One proposal is that the Roman emperor Caligula gave him the city about that year. Aretas IV's reign ended in AD 40.
